headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate to 4% as inflation climbs

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge for loans and pay on savings.
The Monetary Policy Committee, the nine-member Bank of England group that votes on interest rates.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate to 4% as inflation climbs
levels.body:
The Bank of England is due to announce its latest interest rate decision today, 5 November, and markets strongly expect it to raise Bank Rate by 25 basis points from 3.75% to 4%. The outcome was not available when this edition was compiled.
In September the Monetary Policy Committee held the rate at 3.75% by six votes to three, with the three dissenters wanting a rise to 4%. Governor Andrew Bailey said that the longer volatility persists, the more likely the Bank will need to raise rates.
UK inflation, as measured by the Consumer Prices Index, jumped to 3.5% in the 12 months to September from 3.1% in August, driven largely by motor fuel costs. According to LSEG data cited by CNBC in October, traders put the chance of a rise in November at 98%, with most also expecting another in December. Trading Economics lists a consensus forecast of 4%.
levels.why: Bank Rate sets the tone for mortgage, loan and savings rates across the UK economy.

levels.headline: Bank of England set to lift interest rates as prices rise faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England announces its interest rate decision today, 5 November, and the City widely expects it to lift Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. The result was not known when this edition was compiled.
The Monetary Policy Committee voted six to three to hold rates in September, but three members already wanted a rise to 4%. Governor Andrew Bailey warned that if volatility continued, the Bank would be more likely to need to raise rates.
Since then, official figures showed consumer price inflation rising to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, mostly because of higher fuel prices. Traders told LSEG in October that they saw a 98% chance of a rise this month, and many expect a further increase in December. Trading Economics shows a consensus forecast of 4% for today's decision.
levels.why: Interest rate changes feed into mortgages, business loans and savings accounts.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates today
levels.body:
The Bank of England will announce today, 5 November, whether it changes interest rates. Most investors expect it to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. We did not know the result when this edition was put together.
In September, the nine members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted six to three to keep the rate unchanged. The three who lost the vote wanted a rise. Governor Andrew Bailey said that the longer prices stay unstable, the more likely it is that the Bank will have to raise rates.
Inflation, the rate at which prices rise, went up to 3.5% in the year to September, from 3.1% a month earlier, helped by pricier fuel. Market data suggested that traders thought a rise this month was almost certain, and many expect another in December.
levels.why: A higher Bank Rate usually makes borrowing more expensive and saving more rewarding.

levels.headline: Bank of England likely to raise interest rates
levels.body:
The Bank of England is expected to raise its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4% when it announces its decision today, 5 November. The result was not known when this was written.
In September the Bank's rate-setting committee voted six to three to leave rates alone, but the three who disagreed wanted a rise. The Bank's Governor, Andrew Bailey, said rates would be more likely to rise the longer uncertainty over prices continued.
UK inflation reached 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August, mainly because of higher fuel costs. Inflation measures how fast prices rise over a year. Traders think a rise is almost certain this month, and many also expect another in December.
The rate matters because it affects what banks charge on mortgages and loans.
levels.why: Higher rates affect anyone with a loan, a mortgage or savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to put up interest rates today
levels.body:
The Bank of England will say today, 5 November, whether it is changing interest rates. Almost everyone expects it to raise the main rate, called Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%. We did not know the answer when this was written.
Last time, in September, a group of nine experts voted six to three to keep the rate as it was. The three who lost wanted a rise. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said a rise becomes more likely the longer prices keep jumping around.
Prices are going up faster. Inflation, which means the speed prices rise, hit 3.5% in September, up from 3.1%. Higher fuel costs were a big reason. Raising rates is one way the Bank tries to slow price rises down.
levels.why: The rate affects how much people pay on loans and earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England is likely to raise interest rates today
levels.body:
The Bank of England decides today, 5 November, what to do with interest rates. Most experts think it will raise the main rate from 3.75% to 4%. We did not know the result when this was written.
The Bank sets this rate to keep price rises under control. In September, nine Bank experts voted. Six wanted no change and three wanted a rise. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said a rise gets more likely if prices stay unsettled.
Prices are now rising faster. The rate of price rises, called inflation, went from 3.1% to 3.5% over the year to September. Dearer fuel was a main cause. When the Bank raises its rate, borrowing gets dearer, so people tend to spend less, and that can slow price rises.
levels.why: Mortgages, loans and savings can all change when the Bank moves its rate.

levels.headline: The Bank of England may put interest rates up today
levels.body:
Today, 5 November, the Bank of England says what it will do with interest rates. Many people expect it to put the main rate up from 3.75% to 4%. We did not know the result when this was written.
The Bank's job is to stop prices rising too fast. Prices have been rising faster lately. This is called inflation. It went up to 3.5% in the year to September. A month before it was 3.1%. Fuel costs went up a lot.
In September, nine experts at the Bank voted on what to do. Six said keep the rate the same. Three said raise it. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said a rise is more likely if prices stay bumpy. A higher rate makes loans cost more, which can cool spending.
levels.why: It could change what families pay on mortgages and loans.

levels.headline: Will the Bank of England make borrowing cost more today?
levels.body:
The Bank of England tells us today, 5 November, if it will change its interest rate. Lots of people think it will go up. We did not know the answer when this was written.
An interest rate is the price of borrowing money. If you borrow, you pay extra back. The Bank sets a main rate, and banks use it to set their own. Now it is 3.75%. Experts think it may go to 4%.
The Bank does this to keep prices steady. Prices are going up quickly. That is called inflation. It is now 3.5% a year. That means something that cost one pound last year costs about one pound and three and a half pence now. When borrowing costs more, people often spend less, and prices can calm down.
levels.why: Higher rates can mean bigger repayments for people who owe money.

levels.headline: Why a bank might make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
Today the Bank of England decides about something called the interest rate. Lots of people think it will go up a little.
The interest rate is like a fee for borrowing. Imagine you borrow a pound from a friend and give back a pound and a little extra. That little extra is interest. The Bank of England sets a rate that other banks follow. Right now it is 3.75%. It may go to 4%.
Why do this? Prices in shops are going up faster than before. Grown-ups call that inflation. Petrol costs more, and that is part of the reason. If borrowing costs more, people spend less, and then prices tend to stop climbing so fast. Nobody knew the answer when this was written.
levels.why: It helps keep the cost of things steady for families.

levels.headline: A big decision about borrowing money
levels.body:
Today some grown-ups at the Bank of England make a decision about money. They may make borrowing a bit more costly.
Think of it like pocket money. Say you borrow some from a friend and promise to give back a bit extra. That extra is called interest. The Bank of England chooses a level of interest that banks follow across the country. It is 3.75 now. It may go up to 4.
Why would they do that? Things in shops cost more than before. If everyone spends a bit less, prices stop rising so fast, like when fewer children want the same sweets and the shop lowers the price. We do not know yet what they chose.
levels.why: It is about keeping the price of everyday things fair.

headline: S&P 500 closes up 1.58% as Dow posts best day since April 2025 after Democratic midterm win

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies, used as a gauge of the whole market.
The return investors get for lending to the US government; they fall when bond prices rise.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes up 1.58% as Dow posts best day since April 2025 after Democratic midterm win
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up on Wednesday 4 November, the last completed session, rising 1.58% to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,569.40 points, or 3.03%, to close at 53,356.12, its best day since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.44% to 25,736.51, according to CNBC; Trading Economics reports a different Nasdaq figure, so that number is the least certain.
CNBC attributed the rally to Democratic gains in the midterm elections and a sharp fall in oil prices. West Texas Intermediate crude fell more than 8% to settle at $88.12 a barrel.
The moves came after earlier volatility: the Nasdaq had suffered its worst day since June on 29 October as investors sold technology shares. US stock markets were due to reopen later today for Thursday's session.
levels.why: Wall Street's reaction shows how politics and oil prices are shaping investor confidence.

levels.headline: Wall Street surges: S&P 500 up 1.58%, Dow up more than 3%
levels.body:
US shares rose sharply on Wednesday 4 November, the latest completed session. The S&P 500 climbed 1.58% to close at 7,688.62. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1,569.40 points, or 3.03%, to finish at 53,356.12, its best day since April 2025. CNBC reports the Nasdaq Composite up 1.44% at 25,736.51, though another source quotes a different Nasdaq move.
CNBC linked the rally to the Democrats' strong midterm showing and falling oil. West Texas Intermediate crude dropped more than 8% to $88.12 a barrel, easing worries about fuel costs and inflation.
The gains followed a choppy few days, including a technology sell-off on 29 October that gave the Nasdaq its worst day since June. The Dow closed back above 53,000 for the first time since early September.
levels.why: Big swings in US markets can affect pension funds and savings invested in shares.

levels.headline: US stocks jump after midterms as oil prices fall
levels.body:
US stocks closed higher on Wednesday 4 November, the last full trading day. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big US companies, rose 1.58% to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones index jumped 3.03%, or 1,569.40 points, to 53,356.12, its best day since April 2025. The Nasdaq, heavy with technology firms, rose 1.44% to 25,736.51.
CNBC said investors were cheered by the Democrats' strong results in the midterm elections and by a sharp drop in the oil price. US crude oil fell more than 8% to $88.12 a barrel, which eased worries about high fuel costs.
It followed a rough week for tech shares. The Nasdaq had its worst day since June on 29 October after investors sold technology stocks.
levels.why: Falling oil prices can help households and firms by easing costs.

levels.headline: US shares rise sharply after the midterm elections
levels.body:
American shares rose strongly on Wednesday 4 November, the most recent day of trading. The S&P 500, an index of 500 large US companies, closed up 1.58% at 7,688.62. The Dow Jones, another index, rose 3.03% to 53,356.12, its best day since April 2025. The Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, gained 1.44% to 25,736.51.
CNBC said two things helped. Democrats did well in the midterm elections, and the price of US crude oil fell more than 8% to $88.12 a barrel. Cheaper oil can ease inflation, which is the rate prices rise.
The jump came after a bumpy few days. On 29 October, tech shares were sold off and the Nasdaq had its worst day since June.
levels.why: Share prices reflect how confident investors feel about the economy.

levels.headline: US share prices go up after elections and cheaper oil
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States went up a lot on Wednesday 4 November, the last day the market was open. The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 big US firms, rose 1.58% to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones index rose 3.03% to 53,356.12, its best day since April 2025. The Nasdaq, which is full of tech firms, rose 1.44% to 25,736.51.
CNBC said investors liked two things. Democrats did well in the midterm elections. Also, oil got cheaper. US crude fell more than 8% to $88.12 a barrel. Cheaper oil can mean cheaper fuel and lower costs for firms.
The rise followed a bad patch. On 29 October, investors sold many tech shares, and the Nasdaq had its worst day since June.
levels.why: Prices in the stock market can affect people's pensions and savings.

levels.headline: US shares rise sharply after elections and cheaper oil
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States rose sharply on Wednesday 4 November, the latest day the market was open. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, closed up 1.58% at 7,688.62. The Dow Jones rose 3.03% to 53,356.12, its best day since April 2025. The Nasdaq, full of tech firms, rose 1.44% to 25,736.51.
CNBC said investors were pleased that the Democrats did well in the midterm elections. They also liked a big fall in the price of oil. US crude fell more than 8% to $88.12 a barrel, and cheaper oil can mean lower fuel costs.
The rise came after a bad few days for tech shares. On 29 October, investors sold many of them, and the Nasdaq had its worst day since June.
levels.why: Share prices affect many people's pensions and savings.

levels.headline: US share prices jump as oil gets cheaper
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States jumped on Wednesday 4 November, the latest day the market was open. A share is a small piece of a company. An index follows lots of shares together. The S&P 500 follows 500 big companies. It rose 1.58% to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones index rose 3.03% to 53,356.12. The Nasdaq rose 1.44% to 25,736.51.
CNBC said investors were happy about two things. The Democrats did well in the elections held on 3 November. And oil, which is used to make petrol, became much cheaper. US oil fell by more than 8% to $88.12 a barrel.
Just days before, tech companies' shares fell sharply. So this was a big bounce back.
levels.why: Many pensions and savings are tied to share prices.

levels.headline: Why share prices shot up in America
levels.body:
Share prices in America went up a lot on Wednesday 4 November. A share is a tiny slice of a company. People buy and sell shares, and prices go up and down each day. An index is a score that follows many shares at once. The S&P 500 follows 500 big companies, and it went up 1.58%. The Dow Jones is another score, and it went up 3.03%. The Nasdaq went up 1.44%.
Why? Newspaper reports said investors liked the result of the elections, where the Democrats did well. They also liked that oil got cheaper. Oil is used to make petrol. The price of US oil dropped by more than 8%. When fuel costs less, shops and families can feel better about spending.
levels.why: Rising shares can lift pensions, but they can drop again quickly.

levels.headline: Share prices bounce up like a ball
levels.body:
On Wednesday 4 November, share prices in America bounced up. A share is a tiny piece of a company, like owning one slice of a huge pizza. When lots of people want to buy, the price goes up. The big score that follows 500 large companies went up by about one and a half in every hundred. Another score, the Dow, went up by about three in every hundred.
Why did people want to buy? The grown-ups voted in elections, and many liked the result. Also, oil became cheaper. Oil is what makes petrol for cars. When petrol costs less, families have more money left over, a bit like when sweets in the school shop cost less.
levels.why: It shows how happy or worried grown-ups feel about money.

levels.headline: Prices of company pieces went up in America
levels.body:
On Wednesday, the price of little pieces of big American companies went up a lot. These pieces are called shares. Think of a share like a sticker you can swap. When lots of people want your sticker, it is worth more. That is what happened.
Grown-ups in America had just voted in an election, and many were happy with how it turned out. Also, oil got cheaper. Oil makes petrol for cars. When it costs less, shops and families can keep more of their money.
So the main score for 500 big companies went up by about one and a half in every hundred. A second score went up by about three in every hundred. It is like finding extra sweets in your bag.
levels.why: It tells us grown-ups feel more hopeful about money.

headline: Democrats win control of US Congress in midterm rejection of Trump

terms.meaning: Elections held halfway through a US president's term to choose all House seats and about a third of the Senate.
A president's power to block a bill passed by Congress.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of US Congress in midterm rejection of Trump
levels.body:
Democrats have won control of the US Congress in the 3 November midterm elections, according to projections from CNBC and Euronews, though some counts were still changing. Euronews reported Democrats on 220 seats in the 435-seat House, with 218 needed; CNBC's Election Desk projected at least 250.
Democrats were projected to flip Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, and CNBC also named Maine. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by 65 votes with about 95% counted.
A CNBC voter poll found nearly three in four voters said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor. Democrats plan to push a bill to undo Trump's tariffs and to vote again on ending the Iran war, but projections suggest they lack the numbers to override a presidential veto.
levels.why: Control of Congress changes what President Trump can pass on tariffs, spending and war powers.

levels.headline: Democrats sweep Congress as voters punish Trump over Iran war and living costs
levels.body:
Democrats have taken control of the US Congress in the 3 November midterms, according to CNBC and Euronews, although counting was continuing. Euronews put Democrats at 220 House seats, with 218 needed for a majority; CNBC projected at least 250.
In the Senate, Democrats were projected to flip Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, with Maine also named by CNBC. Mississippi was extremely close, with Democrat Scott Colom 65 votes ahead of Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith with around 95% counted.
Euronews linked the result to anger over living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran. A CNBC poll found nearly three in four voters called the war a major factor. Democrats intend to move a bill to undo Trump's tariffs, but they are projected to fall short of a veto-proof majority.
levels.why: The result could reshape US trade policy and the future of the war with Iran.

levels.headline: Democrats win Congress in the US midterm elections
levels.body:
Democrats have won control of the US Congress in the midterm elections held on 3 November, according to CNBC and Euronews. Some votes were still being counted. Euronews said Democrats held 220 of the 435 House seats, where 218 are needed to win. CNBC projected at least 250.
Democrats were expected to take Senate seats from Republicans in six states, including Texas and Ohio. One Mississippi race was so close that Democrat Scott Colom led by only 65 votes.
Euronews said voters were angry about rising living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran. A CNBC poll found nearly three in four voters said the war mattered a lot. Democrats want to cancel Trump's tariffs and end the war, but Trump can veto laws, and Democrats are projected to lack the numbers to overrule him.
levels.why: It limits how freely the president can act on taxes, trade and war.

levels.headline: Democrats take control of Congress in US elections
levels.body:
The Democratic Party has won control of the US Congress in elections held on 3 November, according to CNBC and Euronews. Counting was still going on in some places. The House of Representatives has 435 seats and a party needs 218 to win. Euronews said Democrats had 220, and CNBC projected at least 250.
In the Senate, Democrats were expected to take seats from Republicans in six states, including Texas and Ohio. One race in Mississippi was extremely close, with the Democrat ahead by just 65 votes.
Voters said they were worried about high prices, tariffs and the war with Iran. Democrats say they will try to end the war and cancel Trump's tariffs. But the president can veto laws, and Democrats are not expected to have enough votes to overrule him.
levels.why: It changes how much power President Trump has at home.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of the US Congress
levels.body:
The Democratic Party has won control of Congress, the part of the US government that makes laws. The elections took place on 3 November. These are called midterms because they come halfway through a president's time in office. Some votes were still being counted.
Congress has two parts. The House has 435 seats, and a party needs 218 to win. Euronews said the Democrats had 220. In the Senate, they were expected to take seats from Republicans in six states, including Texas and Ohio.
News reports said voters were upset about high prices, tariffs, and the war with Iran. The Democrats want to end the war and cancel the tariffs. But President Trump can say no to laws. This is called a veto, and the Democrats are not expected to have enough votes to overrule him.
levels.why: The president now has to deal with a Congress run by the other party.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of Congress in US elections
levels.body:
The Democratic Party has won control of the US Congress in elections held on 3 November, according to CNBC and Euronews. Some votes were still being counted. The House of Representatives has 435 seats and a party needs 218 to be in charge. Euronews said Democrats had 220, and CNBC projected at least 250.
In the Senate, Democrats were expected to take seats from Republicans in six states, including Texas and Ohio. One race in Mississippi was so close that the Democrat led by just 65 votes.
Voters said they were upset about high prices, tariffs and the war with Iran. The Democrats want to end the war and cancel the tariffs, but the president can veto laws. Democrats are not expected to have enough votes to overrule him.
levels.why: It changes how much the president can do without the other party.

levels.headline: Democrats win the US elections for Congress
levels.body:
The Democrats have won control of Congress, which is the group that makes laws in the United States. The election was on 3 November. It is called a midterm because it comes halfway through the president's time in charge. Votes were still being counted in some places.
The House has 435 seats. A party needs 218 to be in charge. Euronews said Democrats had 220. In the Senate, the Democrats were expected to win seats from the Republicans in six states, such as Texas and Ohio.
News reports said many voters were upset about rising prices, taxes on imports called tariffs, and a war with Iran. The Democrats want to stop the war and the tariffs. But the president can block laws with a veto, and the Democrats are not expected to have enough votes to beat that.
levels.why: It could change US decisions on trade and war.

levels.headline: Democrats win big in America's elections
levels.body:
Voters in the United States have chosen the Democratic Party to run Congress. Congress is the group of people who make laws for the country. The vote was on 3 November. The president, Donald Trump, belongs to the Republican Party, so now the two sides are not on the same team.
Congress has two halves, the House and the Senate. The Democrats won the House and were expected to win the Senate too. Some votes were still being counted.
Many voters said they were upset about prices going up and about a war with Iran. The Democrats want to end the war. The president can still say no to new laws, and that is called a veto. The Democrats probably do not have enough votes to overrule him.
levels.why: It means the president can no longer do whatever he likes.

levels.headline: The grown-ups in America pick a new team to lead Congress
levels.body:
People in America have voted for who should make laws. The group that makes the laws is called Congress. Until now it was led by the Republican team. This week, voters chose the Democrat team to lead it instead.
Think of it like picking captains at school. The president, Donald Trump, is on the Republican side. Now the other team is in charge of the law-making group. That means he has to work with them, or he cannot get things done.
Many voters said they were upset that things in shops cost more, and that America is in a war with Iran. The new team says it wants to try to stop the war. The president can still say no to new rules, so there may be arguments.
levels.why: It shows that voters can change who is in charge by voting.

levels.headline: The people of America vote for a new team
levels.body:
Lots of grown-ups in America voted this week. They were choosing who should run the group that makes the rules for the whole country. That group is called Congress.
Before, one team ran it. Now a different team has won. It is a bit like when a new class captain is picked, and everyone has to listen to a new person in charge.
The president is the boss of the whole country, and he is on the old team. So now he has to talk with the new team if he wants things to change.
Many people voted because things in the shops cost more than before. Some also wanted a war to stop. Now they wait to see what the new team does.
levels.why: Votes can change who makes the rules.

headline: Healey's Budget extends zero VAT on electricity, raises bank tax and fully funds defence plan

terms.meaning: The government's yearly statement setting out taxes and spending.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the UK economy and public finances.

levels.headline: Healey's Budget extends zero VAT on electricity, raises bank tax and fully funds defence plan
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered the Autumn Budget on 28 October, with measures to cut energy costs, tax banks and raise defence spending, according to CNBC and GOV.UK.
The 0% VAT rate on domestic electricity is extended to July 2027, expected to cut about £50 from the April 2027 Ofgem price cap. A £100 Household Energy Payment, costing £2.6 billion, goes to households in council tax bands A to D in England from January 2027.
The Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge rises from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027, raising £1.5 billion. The £15 billion Defence Investment Plan is fully funded, taking defence spending to 2.7% of GDP in 2027-28. The OBR raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.2%. CNBC said the bank tax rise was milder than feared and London-listed lenders' shares rose.
levels.why: The Budget decides who pays and who benefits from government help with the cost of living.

levels.headline: Budget: energy bill help, a bank tax rise and more money for defence
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey presented the Autumn Budget on 28 October, aiming to ease energy bills, tax banks and boost defence, according to CNBC and GOV.UK.
Zero VAT on domestic electricity is extended to July 2027, which should take roughly £50 off the April 2027 Ofgem price cap. Households in council tax bands A to D in England will get a £100 payment from January 2027, at a cost of £2.6 billion.
Banks face a higher surcharge on corporation tax, rising from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027, raising £1.5 billion. The £15 billion Defence Investment Plan is fully funded, lifting defence spending to 2.7% of GDP in 2027-28. The Office for Budget Responsibility now expects 1.2% growth in 2026. Bank shares rose because the tax rise was smaller than feared.
levels.why: It affects household bills and the cost of running the UK's banks and armed forces.

levels.headline: Budget cuts energy costs, taxes banks and funds defence
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his Budget on 28 October, with help for energy bills, a higher tax on banks and more money for defence, according to CNBC and GOV.UK.
The zero rate of VAT on household electricity continues until July 2027, which should lower the April 2027 energy price cap by about £50. Households in council tax bands A to D in England will get £100 from January 2027.
Banks will pay more tax. A surcharge on their profits rises from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027, raising £1.5 billion. The government also fully funded its £15 billion defence plan, taking defence spending to 2.7% of the economy by 2027-28. The independent forecaster, the OBR, now expects the economy to grow 1.2% this year. Bank shares rose, as the tax rise was less than some had feared.
levels.why: Households and firms feel Budget choices in their bills and taxes.

levels.headline: UK Budget: help with energy bills, and banks to pay more tax
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, set out the government's Budget on 28 October. It included help with energy bills, a higher tax on banks, and more money for the armed forces.
VAT on household electricity stays at zero until July 2027. That should cut around £50 from the April 2027 cap on energy prices. Some households, those in council tax bands A to D in England, will get £100 from January 2027.

The £15 billion plan for defence is now fully paid for, taking defence spending to 2.7% of the economy in 2027-28. The independent forecaster, the OBR, expects growth of 1.2% this year. Bank shares rose as the rise was milder than feared.
levels.why: It affects energy bills, bank profits and government priorities.

levels.headline: Budget: smaller energy bills, higher bank taxes, more for defence
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, told Parliament about the Budget on 28 October. A Budget is when the government says how it will raise and spend money.
Households will keep paying no VAT on electricity until July 2027. This should cut about £50 from energy bills in April 2027. Homes in council tax bands A to D in England will also get £100 from January 2027.

levels.headline: Budget: help with energy bills, and banks to pay more tax
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, set out the government's plans for money on 28 October. This yearly plan is called the Budget. It says how much tax people and firms will pay and what the government will spend.
One change keeps VAT, a tax on sales, at zero on household electricity until July 2027. This should take around £50 off the energy price cap in April 2027. Homes in council tax bands A to D in England will get £100 from January 2027.

levels.why: Budgets decide who pays tax and how help is given.

levels.headline: The Budget: help with energy bills, and banks pay more tax
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, shared the government's plans for money on 28 October. This yearly plan is called the Budget. It says what taxes will be and what the government will spend.
One plan keeps VAT, a sales tax, at zero on household electricity until July 2027. That should take around £50 off energy bills in April 2027. Homes in council tax bands A to D in England will get £100 from January 2027.

levels.why: It can make household bills lower and decide who pays more tax.

levels.headline: The country makes a plan for money

Once a year, the people who run the country make a plan for money. It is called the Budget. Think of it like planning how to use pocket money for the whole year.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September as fuel costs surge

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast the prices of everyday goods and services are rising.
Inflation leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, which can swing sharply.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September as fuel costs surge
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. The figures were published on 21 October, and CNBC described the reading as hotter than expected, driven by the cost of motor fuels.
Core CPI, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.8% from 2.6% in August. Trading Economics put energy inflation at 17.9%, up from 13.8% the month before.
CNBC said the figure cemented expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates, which it is due to decide on today. The next ONS inflation release is due on 18 November.
levels.why: Rising prices reduce what wages and savings can buy, and they drive Bank of England decisions.

levels.headline: Inflation jumps to 3.5% as energy and fuel prices bite
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK climbed to 3.5% in the year to September 2026 from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics reported on 21 October. CNBC called it hotter than expected, blaming surging motor fuel costs.
A measure of core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, suggesting price pressures were broadening a little beyond energy. Trading Economics reported energy inflation of 17.9%, against 13.8% in August.
CNBC said the data cemented expectations of an interest rate rise by the Bank of England, whose decision is due today. The next set of figures from the ONS will be published on 18 November.
levels.why: Higher inflation squeezes household budgets and increases pressure on the Bank to act.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% as fuel gets dearer
levels.body:
The cost of living rose faster in the year to September. The Office for National Statistics said inflation was 3.5%, up from 3.1% in August. CNBC said the figure was higher than economists expected and was driven mostly by dearer petrol and diesel.
A second measure, called core inflation, leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco because their prices jump around. It also went up, to 2.8% from 2.6%. Trading Economics said energy prices were rising at 17.9% a year, faster than 13.8% the month before.
The numbers made an interest rate rise from the Bank of England more likely. It announces its decision today. The ONS will publish the next figures on 18 November.
levels.why: It means prices in shops and at the pump are rising faster than wages may be.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% because of fuel costs
levels.body:
Prices in the UK rose faster in September. The Office for National Statistics said inflation, the rate at which prices rise over a year, was 3.5%. In August it was 3.1%. CNBC said this was higher than expected and was mainly down to more costly petrol and diesel.
A second measure, core inflation, leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, whose prices can swing a lot. It rose from 2.6% to 2.8%. One source said energy prices were up 17.9% over the year.
The rise made it more likely that the Bank of England will raise interest rates. It announces its decision today. The next official figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: People's money buys less when prices rise faster.

levels.headline: UK prices are rising faster, mainly because of fuel

Prices in the UK went up faster in September. The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things, said inflation was 3.5% over the year. A month earlier it was 3.1%. There is also a second count, called core inflation. It leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, because their prices jump about. That count went up too, from 2.6% to 2.8%.
This makes it more likely that the Bank of England will raise interest rates. It tells us its decision today. The next official count is on 18 November.
levels.why: Faster price rises mean money does not stretch as far.

levels.headline: UK prices rise faster, mainly because of fuel

Prices in the UK rose faster in the year to September. The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things, said inflation was 3.5%. A month earlier it was 3.1%. Inflation means how fast prices go up over a year. At 3.5%, something that cost £100 a year ago would now cost about £103.50.

levels.headline: UK prices rose faster in September

levels.why: It affects how far pocket money, wages and savings go.

levels.headline: Why things cost more now
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are going up faster. Grown-ups use the word inflation for this. The Office for National Statistics counts it every month. It said that in the year to September, prices went up by 3.5%. In August, they went up by 3.1%.
Here is an example. A game that cost £100 last year would cost about £103.50 now. Not everything goes up the same amount.
The biggest cause was petrol and diesel, which cost much more. Experts at CNBC said the rise was bigger than they expected.
When prices rise quickly, the Bank of England can raise interest rates to slow them down. It will say what it has chosen today.
levels.why: It helps explain why shopping and fuel feel more costly.

levels.headline: Prices going up and up
levels.body:
Prices in shops are going up. Grown-ups call it inflation. Last month they told us how fast it was happening. For one year, prices went up by 3.5%. The month before it was 3.1%.
Here is an easy way to think of it. If a toy cost £100 last year, now it costs a bit over £103. That is not a lot, but it grows every year if wages do not grow too.
The biggest reason was that petrol and diesel cost more. They are what cars use.
There is a bank, called the Bank of England, that tries to keep prices steady. Today it decides what to do.
levels.why: It shows why money can buy a bit less than before.

levels.headline: Some things cost a bit more
levels.body:
Some things in shops cost more than they did last year. Grown-ups call this inflation. They checked how much more things cost. It was a bit more than before.
It is like the school tuck shop. Say a snack cost £1 last year. Now it costs a little over £1. If this happens to lots of things, your pocket money buys less.
The main reason this time was that petrol and diesel cost more. Petrol is what many cars drink.
There is a big bank, called the Bank of England. It tries to stop prices from rising too fast. Today it will decide what to do next.
levels.why: It explains why pocket money may buy less.

headline: US reportedly strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as Vance says diplomacy remains possible

terms.meaning: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil is shipped.
A neutral country or person who helps two sides talk and reach agreement.

levels.headline: US reportedly strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as Vance says diplomacy remains possible
levels.body:
The United States reportedly struck Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday 2 November, while both sides said talks were still alive, according to CNBC and Euronews. A US official told MS Now it was a defensive measure after Iranians used surface-to-air missiles against US assets. CENTCOM issued no formal statement, and no Iranian official formally confirmed a direct attack.
Vice President JD Vance said Washington had set no deadline for a deal and was hopeful of a negotiated settlement, though Trump keeps military options open. Qatar and Pakistan are mediating, and Qatar said proposals were being exchanged and it still saw hope.
Iran says its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz must be met first, with nuclear talks only afterwards. Parliament speaker Ghalibaf warned of a new battlefield in the war. Diplomacy has repeatedly broken down earlier this year.
levels.why: The war has pushed up fuel prices worldwide and shaped the US midterm vote.

levels.headline: US strike on Iranian island clouds hopes of a deal
levels.body:
The US reportedly carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday 2 November, as mediators worked on a deal, CNBC and Euronews reported. A US official called it a defensive measure after Iranians fired surface-to-air missiles at US assets. There was no formal statement from CENTCOM and no formal Iranian confirmation.
Vice President JD Vance said there is no deadline for a peace deal and that Washington hopes for a negotiated settlement, while Trump keeps military options. Qatar and Pakistan are mediating, and Qatar said there was still hope as proposals were exchanged.
Iran insists the Strait of Hormuz will reopen only on its terms, with nuclear talks to follow. Parliament speaker Ghalibaf warned of a new battlefield. Talks have collapsed several times before this year.
levels.why: The outcome affects oil prices, inflation and global security.

levels.headline: US reportedly hits Iranian island while talks continue
levels.body:
The United States reportedly struck Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday 2 November while peace talks were going on, CNBC and Euronews said. A US official told MS Now that it was defensive, after Iranians used missiles against US forces. The US military has not confirmed it, and Iran has not formally confirmed an attack.
Vice President JD Vance said America has no deadline for a deal and hopes for an agreement through talks, though President Trump still has military choices. Qatar and Pakistan are acting as go-betweens. Qatar said it still saw hope.
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for oil, will reopen only once its conditions are met, with nuclear talks after that. A senior Iranian politician warned of a new battlefield. Past rounds of talks this year have failed.
levels.why: It affects fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: US reportedly strikes an Iranian island as talks go on

levels.why: The war affects oil prices and the cost of living around the world.

levels.headline: US reportedly hits Iranian island as talks to end war continue

levels.why: It affects the price of petrol and the risk of a bigger war.

levels.headline: The war with Iran: an attack, and some hope
levels.body:
The United States and Iran have been in a war for months. On Monday 2 November, news reports said the US attacked an Iranian island called Qeshm. A US official said it was to protect US soldiers. Nobody official has fully confirmed it.

levels.headline: Two countries in a war, and some friends trying to help

levels.why: It shows why far-away wars can change prices at home.

levels.headline: Two grown-up countries arguing, and friends trying to help

But two other countries, Qatar and Pakistan, are trying to help them stop. It is like when a teacher asks two friends to say sorry and make up.
Iran is in charge of a narrow sea road that ships use to carry oil. Oil is used to make petrol for cars. Iran says it will open the road when the US agrees to its rules.
So far, they have not agreed.
levels.why: Wars can make things more costly for everyone.

headline: MPs warn Parliament risks 'catastrophic failure' as restoration delay adds £420m a year

terms.meaning: Moving MPs and peers out of the Palace of Westminster so repair work can be done.

levels.headline: MPs warn Parliament risks 'catastrophic failure' as restoration delay adds £420m a year
levels.body:
MPs on Parliament's public accounts committee warned on Wednesday 4 November that the continuing delay to restoring the Palace of Westminster puts it at risk of a major failure, according to Euronews. The committee chair cited a risk that the chamber could be plunged into darkness during the State Opening of Parliament.
Each year of delay adds about £420 million to the lifetime cost of the scheme. A June 2026 National Audit Office update gave a range of £320 million to £420 million a year.
The building suffers from crumbling masonry, ageing electrics, frequent leaks and high levels of asbestos. The delay stems from MPs failing to agree how to proceed. Parliamentarians voted in 2018 to move out for repairs. A full decant would cost up to £15.6 billion and take between 19 and 24 years. Both houses are expected to vote on a plan later this year.
levels.why: Delay is raising the bill for taxpayers and the risk to the home of UK democracy.

headline: Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action ban as police make arrests outside

levels.headline: Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action ban as police make arrests outside
levels.body:
The UK Supreme Court began hearing an appeal on Wednesday 4 November against the government's ban on Palestine Action, with the two-day hearing continuing on Thursday. Euronews reported that police arrested supporters of the group outside the court. No judgment has been given.
The appeal is brought by co-founder Huda Ammori. She was granted permission to challenge the ban on a narrow procedural ground, namely that the Home Office allegedly did not follow its own criteria.
The ban came into force on 5 July 2025 and makes membership or support of the group a criminal offence carrying up to 14 years in prison. The High Court found the proscription disproportionate in February, but the Court of Appeal reversed that in June. Euronews says charges linked to the ban could be affected if the appeal succeeds.
levels.why: The case tests how far the state can go in banning a protest group as terrorist.

headline: Oil prices fall for a second day on hopes of a diplomatic end to the Iran war

levels.headline: Oil prices fall for a second day on hopes of a diplomatic end to the Iran war
levels.body:
Oil prices fell sharply in the first days of November as markets hoped for a diplomatic end to the US-Iran war, CNBC reported. Brent crude, the international benchmark, settled $8.66, or 7.63%, lower at $104.77 a barrel on Monday 2 November, then shed another $1.17 to $103.60 on Tuesday. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate lost 37 cents to $96.09 on Tuesday.
On Wednesday 4 November, as Democrats won big in the US midterms, WTI fell more than 8% to settle at $88.12 a barrel, according to CNBC's stock market coverage. Prices briefly rose on reports of a US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman said Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion. Higher oil prices have fed into fuel costs and inflation in the UK, euro zone and elsewhere.
levels.why: Oil prices feed directly into petrol costs, energy bills and inflation.

levels.headline: Why the price of oil dropped this week

levels.why: Oil prices touch almost everything we buy.

levels.headline: Why the cost of petrol can go up and down
levels.body:
Cars and lorries need petrol or diesel to move. Both are made from oil. The price of oil changed a lot this week. It got cheaper.
Why? There is a war between the United States and Iran, in the part of the world where lots of oil comes from. When grown-ups worry that there will not be enough oil, the price goes up. This week they felt more hopeful that the war might end, so the price came down.

levels.why: It can change what families pay for fuel and food.

levels.headline: Why petrol can cost more or less
levels.body:

There is a war in a place where lots of oil comes from. When people worry about the war, oil costs more. It is like a sweet that everyone suddenly wants, so the shop raises the price. This week people felt more hopeful that the war might end. So the price of oil fell.
When oil costs less, petrol can cost less too. Lorries that bring food to shops can save money. Then the food might cost a little less too.
But it can change again quickly.
levels.why: Prices for fuel and food depend on faraway events.

headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for the first time in three years as ECB rate hike looms

terms.meaning: The group of European Union countries that use the euro as their currency.

levels.headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for the first time in three years as ECB rate hike looms
levels.body:
Euro zone inflation rose to 4% in the 12 months to October, up from 3.8% in September, according to the flash estimate released on 4 November. CNBC and Euronews said it is the highest reading since September 2023, when it was 4.3%.
Energy prices ran 20.8% above a year earlier, adding roughly 1.9 percentage points to the headline figure, with reporting linking this to the Iran war. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held at 2.5%.
Italy's rate jumped to 5.6% from 4.2%, the largest rise, while Germany's fell to 2.8%, mainly because of a fuel tax cut from 1 October.
The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October after raising it in June and September. Markets see about an 84% chance of a quarter-point rise at the 16-17 December meeting.
levels.why: Higher euro zone inflation squeezes households and raises the chance of costlier borrowing across Europe.

levels.why: It makes further ECB rate rises more likely.

levels.headline: Deadly Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia overshadows US-mediated talks planned in Abu Dhabi
levels.body:
